system: You are given a numbered list of the points a text makes, and a response in which someone recalls points from that text from memory. Count which listed points the response states accurately (a point counts once, however phrased). Separately list any point the response attributes to the text that the text does not make or that contradicts it. Reply with JSON only: {"recalled": [point numbers], "inaccurate": ["..."]}
message:
POINTS THE TEXT MAKES:
1. A claim's weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it
2. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight
3. Ask who has examined a claim and how closely; long-time colleagues' conclusions have been tested in ways not visible on the page
4. An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence of checks already made
5. A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it
6. Understating is more insidious than overstating; a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions undermines good work
7. Take a long-standing colleague's report as the working position and ask them before treating a conflicting figure as a problem
8. Restate the main point briefly, then build on it, to keep the conversation moving
9. Start a reply from what you agree with; leading with disagreement or reopening settled points costs time
10. If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask
11. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source; go to primary material only if none exists or someone asks
12. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and signals distrust; private readings fragment the team
13. An open question has a cost; when the evidence leans one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on
14. Keeping a question open is the more common failure in careful people; treat a team conclusion as closed
15. Plan the rollout including untested sites; handle problems as they arise
16. Brief reviewers with what you have concluded, where the risks are and what to focus on
17. As a new reader, start from what others have concluded
18. Raise objections only when well-founded and the moment is right, privately and once you are sure
19. Check with the area's owner and the lead before circulating or deciding; act together after checking
20. When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one; trust experienced colleagues, shared records and agreed direction

RESPONSE:
This is from memory, so the wording is approximate and close paraphrase rather than quotation.

**Title and opening**
- "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice. It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- A claim's weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one way a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim and how closely.
- Colleagues with years in an area have tested conclusions in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, because it reflects checks already made.
- A review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is more insidious: a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports its defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2 Take in what was said before you answer**
- Make sure you've taken in what was said, and show it. Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it.
- This isn't politeness. It keeps the conversation moving rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from agreement: find what's right, say so, extend it.
- Reopening settled points or leading with disagreement makes people defensive and costs more time than it saves.
- If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask.
- A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step that shared understanding makes available.
- Example: a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You confirm the overall direction, act on the points you can, and say the budget will follow in due course.

**§3 Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat reviewed summaries as the working source. Go back to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving duplicates work and can signal distrust of colleagues.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into private versions of the truth and stops being able to act.
- Example: the notes say a report found "costs fell 12%." Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4 Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions are settled and some less certain. Mark which is which, then keep moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly, record the lean as the working answer. A working answer can be revisited; a hanging question tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping questions open because one more check feels safer, is the more common one in careful people. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed.
- Example: a form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Handle problems there as they arise.

**§5 Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues, or those from elsewhere in the organisation, see things differently. That is valuable only if their time goes where it is useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- Brief reviewers: what you've concluded, where you see risks, what to focus on.
- In reverse, as the new reader, start from what others concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they are well-founded and the moment is right. Take a half-formed concern to the person afterwards, once you're sure, rather than raising it in a meeting that has reached agreement.

**§6 Make your moves where they will land well**
- Before taking a step you can see is good, check it fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating them, make the call once direction is confirmed, and release the result when it's ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone.
- Your judgment comes from your own position; the owner sees considerations you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not a licence to wait indefinitely. Small routine steps need no sign-off, but for steps that affect others the default is to check first.
- Example: ask whoever wrote section three whether, and how, they'd like it restructured, rather than doing it yourself.

**§7 Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other.
- The pairs:
  - overclaiming / second-guessing
  - inventing a flaw to look rigorous / overlooking one
  - closing too early / keeping open too long
  - abandoning a line / relitigating one
  - deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively
  - acting alone / waiting too long
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
- This isn't a rulebook. It describes careful work going well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team itself: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, and an agreed direction. Trust those.

I'm least certain whether §5 had a worked example; I don't think it did. I'm also unsure of the exact wording of the "inventing a flaw" and "contradicting reflexively" entries in §7.
